docs.title: Transaction Support
docs.text:
Part of the FluDa toolkit — module source.

FluDa Transaction Support provides container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries backed directly by a standard DataSource or JPA.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Depending on the runtime, applications can participate in database transactions in two ways:

  • Java SE or a Servlet container — use the fluda-tx modules for resource-local transactions. A CDI interceptor honors jakarta.transaction.Transactional over a plain JDBC DataSource, with no JTA required.
  • A full Jakarta EE runtime (WildFly, GlassFish, Payara, Open Liberty, ...) — the container ships a JTA implementation, so jakarta.transaction.Transactional works out of the box and the fluda-tx modules are unnecessary.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Module Description fluda-tx-core Core SPI: PlatformTransactionManager, exceptions, and synchronization infrastructure. fluda-tx-cdi CDI extension and @Transactional interceptor. fluda-tx-jdbc Resource-local DataSourceTransactionManager and TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy. fluda-tx-jpa JPA-based transaction manager with EntityManager integration.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• PlatformTransactionManager — the SPI that abstracts transaction begin/commit/rollback. The fluda-tx-jdbc module provides a DataSourceTransactionManager for resource-local JDBC transactions.
  • TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy — wraps a raw DataSource so that getConnection() returns the transaction-bound connection inside an active transaction, and close() is suppressed.
  • CDI interceptor — auto-registered by fluda-tx-cdi, drives the transaction lifecycle around @Transactional methods.

See the getting started guide to add dependencies and set up a minimal example, the JDBC implementation page for DataSource-based transactions, the JPA implementation page for EntityManager-based transactions, and advanced topics for multiple DataSources and mixing JPA with JDBC.

docs.title: Mixing JDBC and JPA
docs.text:
Because the same physical Connection backs both the EntityManager and the TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy, JPA and JDBC operations share a single transaction:

@ApplicationScoped
public class OrderService {

    @Inject
    EntityManager em;

    @Inject
    JdbcClient client;

    @Transactional
    public void createOrder(Order order) {
        em.persist(order);                                    // JPA
        client.sql("INSERT INTO audit_log (msg) VALUES (:m)") // JDBC
              .param("m", "Order created: " + order.getId())
              .update();
    }
}

This allows you to leverage the strengths of both APIs: JPA for entity management and relationships, JDBC for bulk operations or complex queries that benefit from direct SQL.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide covers adding FluDa Transaction Support to your project and setting up resource-local transactions in a CDI environment.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or later.
  • A CDI container (Weld SE for Java SE, Weld Servlet for Servlet containers, or a full Jakarta EE server).
  • A JDBC DataSource (typically a connection pool like HikariCP).

docs.title: For Java SE or Servlet environments
docs.text:
Add the three tx modules:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-tx-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-tx-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-tx-jdbc</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The tx modules declare the CDI API and jakarta.transaction-api as provided: supply a CDI container (Weld SE, or a Servlet container with Weld) plus jakarta.transaction-api for the @Transactional annotation.

docs.title: For Jakarta EE environments
docs.text: On a full Jakarta EE server, JTA is built in, so jakarta.transaction.Transactional is handled by the container — no fluda-tx dependency is needed. Just use the JDBC Client modules and let the container manage transactions.

docs.title: Setting up transactions
docs.text:
Resource-local transactions require three pieces:

  1. A raw connection pool (e.g. HikariCP)
  2. A TransactionAwareDataSource wrapping the pool — this is the DataSource your code injects
  3. A PlatformTransactionManager implementation built from the same raw pool

docs.title: Wiring the DataSource and transaction manager
docs.text:
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig;
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.PlatformTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.DataSourceTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;

@ApplicationScoped
public class DatabaseConfig {

    private final HikariDataSource pool;

    public DatabaseConfig() {
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        config.setUsername("sa");
        config.setPassword("");
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
        this.pool = new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return new TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy(pool);
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager() {
        return new DataSourceTransactionManager(pool);
    }
}

Important

The DataSourceTransactionManager and the TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy must share the same raw pool — the pool instance is the key that binds the transaction's Connection to the thread.

docs.title: Using @Transactional
docs.text:
Annotate a CDI bean method with jakarta.transaction.Transactional. Inject the transaction-aware DataSource (or JdbcClient) and use it as usual:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;
import jakarta.transaction.Transactional;

@ApplicationScoped
public class OrderService {

    @Inject
    JdbcClient client;

    @Transactional
    public void createOrder(String info) {
        client.sql("INSERT INTO orders (info) VALUES (:info)")
                .param("info", info)
                .update();
    }
}

The CDI interceptor auto-registered by fluda-tx-cdi drives the transaction around the method: it opens a Connection, disables auto-commit, and commits on success or rolls back on failure. Inside the method the proxy returns that bound Connection and suppresses close(), so try-with-resources blocks do not end the transaction prematurely.

docs.title: Transaction propagation
docs.text:
Control propagation with Transactional.TxType (REQUIRED by default):

@Transactional(Transactional.TxType.REQUIRES_NEW)
public void doWork() {
    // always starts a new transaction
}

Supported types: REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, MANDATORY, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED, NEVER.

docs.title: Exception classification
docs.text:
By default the transaction rolls back on RuntimeException or Error, and commits on checked exceptions. Override with rollbackOn and dontRollbackOn:

@Transactional(rollbackOn = CheckedBusinessException.class)
public void doWork() throws CheckedBusinessException {
}

@Transactional(dontRollbackOn = NoRollbackException.class)
public void doWork() {
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: See the JDBC implementation page for DataSource-based transactions and the JPA implementation page for EntityManager-based transactions.

docs.title: JDBC Implementation
docs.text: The fluda-tx-jdbc module provides a resource-local DataSourceTransactionManager and TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy for environments without JTA.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The DataSourceTransactionManager obtains a Connection from the raw pool, disables auto-commit, and binds it to the current thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager. The TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy intercepts getConnection() calls:

  • Inside a transaction — returns the bound Connection and suppresses close() so the transaction is not ended prematurely.
  • Outside a transaction — delegates directly to the raw pool.

docs.title: Using with JDBC Client
docs.text:
The transaction support integrates seamlessly with FluDa JDBC Client. If you want to use the fluent JdbcClient API together with transaction management, add the JDBC Client modules:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>

The TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy works transparently with JdbcClient — when you inject a JdbcClient in a @Transactional method, it automatically uses the transaction-bound connection.

docs.title: Java SE (Weld SE)
docs.text:
Bootstrap Weld SE as usual. The CDI extension in fluda-tx-cdi auto-registers the @Transactional interceptor.

import org.jboss.weld.environment.se.Weld;
import org.jboss.weld.environment.se.WeldContainer;

try (WeldContainer container = new Weld().initialize()) {
    OrderService service = container.select(OrderService.class).get();
    service.createOrder("Java 25 Book");
}

Make sure beans.xml is present in META-INF/ and the DatabaseConfig producer from the getting started guide is on the classpath.

docs.title: Servlet container (Tomcat + Weld)
docs.text:
In a Servlet container, use Weld's servlet integration. The DataSource is typically obtained from JNDI:

import io.github.fludakit.tx.PlatformTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.DataSourceTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;

@ApplicationScoped
public class DatabaseConfig {

    @Resource(name = "jdbc/myDS")
    private DataSource dataSource;

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public DataSource transactionAwareDataSource() {
        return new TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy(dataSource);
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager() {
        return new DataSourceTransactionManager(dataSource);
    }
}

Declare the JNDI DataSource in META-INF/context.xml (Tomcat) or the equivalent for your container.

docs.title: Transaction-phase callbacks
docs.text:
Register a TransactionSynchronization with TransactionSynchronizationManager to run code at a transaction phase. Registration must happen inside an active transaction.

import io.github.fludakit.tx.support.TransactionSynchronization;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.support.TransactionSynchronizationManager;

@Transactional
public void doWork() {
    TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(new TransactionSynchronization() {
        @Override
        public void afterCommit() {
            // commit-only follow-up
        }

        @Override
        public void afterCompletion(CompletionStatus status) {
            // COMMITTED or ROLLED_BACK
        }
    });
}

TransactionSynchronizationManager.setRollbackOnly() marks the current transaction for rollback without throwing.

docs.title: CDI transaction-phase events
docs.text:
Observers can react to the transaction outcome with @Observes(during = TransactionPhase.X). An event fired inside an active transaction is deferred and delivered at the matching phase.

import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.event.Observes;
import jakarta.enterprise.event.TransactionPhase;

@ApplicationScoped
public class OrderNotifier {

    public void onCreated(@Observes(during = TransactionPhase.AFTER_SUCCESS) OrderCreated event) {
        // runs only if the transaction commits
    }
}

Supported phases are BEFORE_COMPLETION, AFTER_SUCCESS, AFTER_FAILURE, and AFTER_COMPLETION. IN_PROGRESS observers fire immediately.

docs.title: JPA Implementation
docs.text: The fluda-tx-jpa module provides a JpaTransactionManager that drives transactions through a standard JPA EntityManagerFactory. It allows mixing JPA operations and plain JDBC SQL within the same @Transactional method, both operating on the same physical connection.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
JpaTransactionManager creates an EntityManager, begins a resource-local EntityTransaction, and extracts the underlying JDBC Connection via a configurable ConnectionExtractor. Both the EntityManager and the Connection are bound to the TransactionContext:

  • EntityManager — bound under the EntityManagerFactory key
  • Connection — bound under the DataSource key, enabling JDBC fallback through TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-tx-jpa</artifactId>
    <version>${fluda.version}</version>
</dependency>

You also need a JPA provider (e.g. Hibernate) and a JDBC DataSource.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Produce an EntityManagerFactory and a JpaTransactionManager as CDI beans:

import io.github.fludakit.tx.PlatformTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jpa.JpaTransactionManager;

@ApplicationScoped
public class JpaConfig {

    private final EntityManagerFactory emf;

    public JpaConfig() {
        this.emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("myPU");
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public EntityManagerFactory entityManagerFactory() {
        return emf;
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public DataSource transactionAwareDataSource(DataSource rawDs) {
        return new TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy(rawDs);
    }

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(DataSource rawDs) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf, rawDs);
    }
}

docs.title: Injecting EntityManager
docs.text:
The EntityManagerProducer (auto-discovered by CDI) provides a transaction-scoped EntityManager proxy via @Inject:

@ApplicationScoped
public class UserService {

    @Inject
    private EntityManager em;

    @Transactional
    public void createUser(User user) {
        em.persist(user);
    }
}

The proxy defers EntityManager lookup until first method invocation, so injection works at bean creation time before any transaction is active.

docs.title: ConnectionExtractor
docs.text:
The JPA spec does not standardize em.unwrap(Connection.class). ConnectionExtractor is a pluggable strategy for extracting the JDBC Connection from an EntityManager.

The DEFAULT extractor tries em.unwrap(Connection.class) first, then falls back to Hibernate's SessionImplementor.getJdbcConnectionAccess() if Hibernate is on the classpath.

For other JPA providers, supply a custom extractor:

public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(DataSource ds) {
    return new JpaTransactionManager(emf, ds, myCustomExtractor);
}

docs.title: JpaHelper
docs.text:
For programmatic access to the current EntityManager:

// Single EntityManagerFactory
EntityManager em = JpaHelper.currentEntityManager();

// Multiple EntityManagerFactories — pass the raw (non-proxy) factory
EntityManager em = JpaHelper.currentEntityManager(emf);

docs.title: The synchronous transaction model
docs.text:
This document describes the design of fludakit-tx after the resource-local redesign. It is deliberately narrow: synchronous, resource-local transactions only. There is no reactive API, no @Async, no distributed/XA coordination, and no connection-pool abstraction layer.

The design borrows its core idea from Micronaut Data's data-tx module (io.micronaut.transaction), specifically the synchronous path: SynchronousTransactionManager, TransactionOperations, TransactionStatus, AbstractTransactionOperations, DefaultTransactionStatus, SavepointManager, TransactionSynchronization. Everything below either mirrors that model or explains why this codebase's version is smaller.

docs.title: The one idea
docs.text:
A transaction is a status object.

There is exactly one object per transaction. It carries the transaction definition, the bound resource, the rollback-only flags, the registered synchronizations, the optional savepoint, and the completion state. That object is what the interceptor creates, what the template binds to the current thread/scope, and what the unit of work receives.

Everything else in the model exists to create, bind, complete, or observe that object:

TransactionDefinition ──┐
                        ├──> TransactionStatus ──> unit of work ──> commit | rollback
            resource ───┘

Consequences:

  • No separate TransactionContext alongside a passive TransactionStatus. That split made the status a record and forced the lifecycle state machine to live somewhere else.
  • No TransactionTemplate owned by the front-ends. The template is the manager itself.
  • Propagation is not a switch over a passive object; the status kind decides what "commit", "rollback", and "setRollbackOnly" mean.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Package Contents Visibility io.github.fludakit.tx API: definition, status, manager, operations, savepoints, exceptions public, application-facing io.github.fludakit.tx.support Runtime: the template, the status implementation, the scope holder, @RawPool, TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy, JdbcConnections public io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc JdbcTransactionManager, JdbcTransactionManagerProducer public io.github.fludakit.tx.jpa JpaTransactionManager, JpaHelper, EntityManagerProducer, the persistence and factory producers, PersistenceConfigurationCustomizer, ConnectionExtractor public io.github.fludakit.tx.cdi @Transactional interceptor, @TransactionScoped context, transactional event dispatch, metadata registry public

Dependencies point one way: jdbc, jpa, cdi → core. core knows nothing about JDBC, JPA, or CDI (the jakarta.enterprise dependency is provided and only used for TransactionScoped type references in documentation).

docs.title: TransactionDefinition
docs.text:
Immutable transaction attributes: propagation (Propagation), rollbackOn / dontRollbackOn, and readOnly.

Propagation carries the six jakarta.transaction.Transactional.TxType behaviours plus NESTED, which Jakarta Transactions deliberately leaves out of the annotation. The CDI front-end resolves the annotation with Propagation.of(TxType); NESTED is reachable only programmatically, through executeNested(...).

It owns the rollback decision: rollbackOn(Throwable) applies the configured rules and falls back to RuntimeException/Error, unwrapping InvocationTargetException and ExecutionException first. This is the rule set the Jakarta @Transactional specification prescribes, and it is also Spring's TransactionTemplate default — so the declarative and the programmatic front-end use the same rule set. They cannot disagree.

withPropagation(...) and withReadOnly(...) return copies; a definition is never mutated.

docs.title: TransactionStatus<T>
docs.text:
The transaction handle. T is the resource type the manager binds (Connection for JDBC, EntityManager for JPA).

definition:       TransactionDefinition
resource:         T?                       // null outside an actual transaction
isNewTransaction: boolean                  // begun here, so completion belongs to this caller
isNestedTransaction: boolean               // savepoint-scoped section inside an outer transaction
isActualTransactionActive: boolean         // false for the shared no-transaction status
isRollbackOnly / isLocalRollbackOnly / isGlobalRollbackOnly
setRollbackOnly()
isCompleted
isSavepointSupported / createSavepoint / rollbackToSavepoint / releaseSavepoint
registerSynchronization(TransactionSynchronization)
getAttribute(Class<A>) / putAttributeIfAbsent(Class<A>, A)   // typed attribute slots

The typed attribute slots exist for exactly two consumers: @TransactionScoped bean stores and the CDI transactional event dispatcher. They are not a general-purpose map.

docs.title: TransactionManager<T>
docs.text:
TransactionManager<T> extends TransactionalOperations<T> — one object, two views. The operations view is what application code and the interceptor use; the manager view is the low-level demarcation API (getTransaction, commit, rollback) used for manual control and by the template itself.

Optional<TransactionStatus<T>> findTransactionStatus();  // the ambient, actual transaction
T getResource();                                         // its resource, or null
<R> R execute(TransactionDefinition, TransactionExecution<T,R>) throws Exception;
TransactionStatus<T> getTransaction(TransactionDefinition);
void commit(TransactionStatus<T>);
void rollback(TransactionStatus<T>);

docs.title: AbstractTransactionOperations<T>
docs.text:
The template. It implements propagation, suspension, begin/complete, synchronization dispatch, and completion state. Concrete managers implement only primitive hooks:

protected abstract void doBegin(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);
protected abstract void doCommit(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);
protected abstract void doRollback(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);

// optional
protected void doNestedBegin(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);    // default: create a savepoint
protected void doNestedCommit(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);    // default: release it
protected void doNestedRollback(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);  // default: roll back to it
protected void doSuspend(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);         // default: no-op
protected void doResume(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status);          // default: no-op
protected SavepointManager newSavepointManager(DefaultTransactionStatus<T> status); // default: null

The hooks receive the concrete DefaultTransactionStatus<T> because they mutate the transaction's own state (resource, savepoint, rollback flags); TransactionStatus stays the read/participate surface for application code.

The default nested hooks use the status's savepoint API, so a manager that supplies a SavepointManager gets NESTED propagation for free.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
execute(definition, work)
  │
  ├─ resolve ambient status
  ├─ dispatch on definition.propagation()
  │
  ├─ join:        work(existing.resource, existing)          // nothing to complete
  ├─ no-tx:       work(null, NO_TRANSACTIONAL)               // SUPPORTS / NOT_SUPPORTED / NEVER
  └─ new tx:      create status ──► bind ──► doBegin
                                     │
                                     ├─ work
                                     ├─ failure && definition.rollbackOn(failure)? rollback : commit
                                     └─ unbind

Completing a new transaction:

  1. already completed → IllegalTransactionStateException
  2. local rollback-only → rollback
  3. global rollback-only (a joined participant marked it) → rollback, then UnexpectedRollbackException (the caller asked for a commit that cannot happen)
  4. beforeCommit(readOnly) → beforeCompletion() → doCommit
  5. afterCommit() → afterCompletion(COMMITTED)
  6. doCleanup is not a hook: managers register a TransactionSynchronization for release, so resource cleanup runs on the same path for every manager and cannot be forgotten.

Failure while committing marks the status UNKNOWN and fires afterCompletion(UNKNOWN); a failure while rolling back does the same. The transaction is completed exactly once.

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
Propagation No ambient transaction Ambient transaction REQUIRED begin join REQUIRES_NEW begin suspend, begin, resume SUPPORTS no-tx status join NOT_SUPPORTED no-tx status suspend, no-tx status, resume MANDATORY IllegalTransactionStateException join NEVER no-tx status TransactionUsageException NESTED begin savepoint-scoped section

join hands the participant a JoinedTransactionStatus view over the running transaction. The view owns nothing: resource, definition, attributes, savepoints, and synchronizations all delegate to the owning status, isNewTransaction() is false, and the participant must not complete the transaction. A rollback-only mark on the view is escalated to the owner as global rollback-only, so the boundary that actually commits cannot silently ignore it. A NESTED section is the other case with its own status object, because it owns a savepoint and its rollback-only flag must stay local.

Suspension is scope-based: the holder restores the outer status when the inner scope closes, so REQUIRES_NEW and NOT_SUPPORTED cannot leak. doSuspend/doResume exist for managers that must detach something physical (for example an OSIV-managed EntityManager); JDBC and JPA in this repository have nothing to detach and leave them as no-ops.

docs.title: Savepoints
docs.text:
SavepointManager is a property of the manager, attached to each new status at begin time. TransactionStatus exposes createSavepoint / rollbackToSavepoint / releaseSavepoint over it, and reports isSavepointSupported().

This is a deliberate change from the old model, where the savepoint manager was passed into a static status factory: the capability now travels with the transaction it belongs to, and NESTED is just the default nested hooks over that capability.

executeNested(work) on TransactionalOperations is the programmatic entry point: it runs NESTED when a transaction is active and a plain REQUIRED transaction otherwise (there is nothing to nest into).

docs.title: Synchronizations
docs.text:
TransactionSynchronization is the callback contract (beforeCommit, beforeCompletion, afterCommit, afterCompletion(Status)), with Status = COMMITTED, ROLLED_BACK, UNKNOWN. This replaces the old TransactionCallback, whose CompletionStatus duplicated the status state.

A synchronization registered on a joined call is attached to the transaction that is actually running (the outer one), so it fires once, at the real boundary. A synchronization registered on a nested section is attached to the outer transaction as well: a savepoint section has no completion of its own.

docs.title: Transactional CDI events
docs.text:
Standard CDI transactional observers — @Observes(during = TransactionPhase.AFTER_SUCCESS), and friends — are the public surface; no annotation of our own is involved. The container drives those observers itself only for JTA transactions, and the transaction model here is resource-local, so the CDI module bridges the gap:

  1. At deployment, TransactionalCdiExtension vetoes every observer whose phase is not IN_PROGRESS and registers one replacement per observer. The replacement keeps the original observed type and qualifier set — so CDI still does the type and qualifier matching — and reports its own phase as IN_PROGRESS.
  2. When an event reaches a replacement, the payload is handed to the transaction's TransactionEventDispatcher together with the observer and its declared phase.
  3. The dispatcher is a TransactionSynchronization that holds the payloads and delivers them at the matching callback:
CDI phase Delivered from When BEFORE_COMPLETION beforeCompletion() before commit or rollback AFTER_SUCCESS afterCommit() after the resource committed AFTER_FAILURE afterCompletion() after a rollback AFTER_COMPLETION afterCompletion() after either outcome

The dispatcher installs itself on the first event of the transaction, bound to the status as a typed attribute, rather than being installed by the interceptor. That is what makes transactional observers work for every boundary: the @Transactional interceptor (5. afterCommit() → afterCompletion(COMMITTED) in the lifecycle above) and a programmatic manager.execute(...) call behave identically. A joined participant and a NESTED section share the attribute and the synchronization registration with the transaction that is actually running, so each event is delivered exactly once, at the real boundary.

An event fired with no actual transaction active is dropped: a transactional observer must not run without a transaction. A failing observer is logged and neither stops the other observers nor changes the transaction's outcome.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
All failures derive from TransactionException extends jakarta.transaction.TransactionalException, so the declarative and programmatic paths satisfy the same contract.

Exception Meaning IllegalTransactionStateException MANDATORY without a transaction; double completion; commit/rollback of a non-owning status TransactionUsageException NEVER inside a transaction NestedTransactionNotSupportedException NESTED without savepoint support UnexpectedRollbackException commit requested for a transaction marked rollback-only TransactionSystemException the resource failed to begin/commit/roll back (wraps the cause)

docs.title: What each module contributes
docs.text:
core — the model above, and nothing else. The scope holder (TransactionStatusHolder) binds the current status per thread: an InheritableThreadLocal carrying a revocable binding on JDK 21, a ScopedValue on JDK 25 (multi-release overlay). The binding is closed when the scope ends, so a transaction never outlives its boundary, even when a raw thread inherited it.

jdbc — JdbcTransactionManager opens a Connection in doBegin (auto-commit off, optional read-only), binds it to the status, and registers a synchronization that resets and closes it. Savepoints map to JDBC savepoints through the shared JdbcSavepointManager, which also tolerates drivers that reject releaseSavepoint. TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy lets plain dataSource.getConnection() code join the transaction; outside one it delegates to the pool, credentials included. JdbcTransactionManagerProducer reuses the application's unqualified TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy when it exposes one, so application code and the manager share a single proxy; otherwise it prefers a @RawPool bean and falls back to the default DataSource, wrapping that pool itself.

jpa — JpaTransactionManager creates an EntityManager, begins its EntityTransaction, binds both the EntityManager and the underlying Connection (so mixed JDBC/JPA code shares one transaction), and flushes on commit. Savepoints are JDBC savepoints over the extracted connection, through the same JdbcSavepointManager.

The manager only borrows an EntityManagerFactory: it never creates, owns, or closes one. Under CDI the container supplies the whole chain:

  • PersistenceConfigurationProducer resolves the raw pool the same way the JDBC producer does (@RawPool first, unqualified DataSource second), but rejects a TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy: a persistence unit has to be built over the pool itself. It binds the pool as jakarta.persistence.nonJtaDataSource and applies every PersistenceConfigurationCustomizer bean. A customizer supplies what only the application knows: managed classes, provider properties, and optionally the persistence unit name.
  • EntityManagerFactoryProducer creates the factory once and closes it at shutdown.
  • JpaTransactionManagerProducer produces the manager over that factory; a ConnectionExtractor bean, when declared, replaces ConnectionExtractor.DEFAULT.

No customizer is required; without one the persistence unit is named __defaultPU and has no managed classes, which suits an application that keeps its mappings in persistence.xml.

In plain Java, build the factory yourself and pass it in:

EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("myPU", Map.of(
        "jakarta.persistence.nonJtaDataSource", pool));
JpaTransactionManager txManager = new JpaTransactionManager(emf);

The DataSource is carried as the jakarta.persistence.nonJtaDataSource property, which is what providers such as Hibernate read in resource-local mode; the factory stays the caller's.

cdi — the interceptor looks up the definition the extension precomputed at deployment (resolving and caching it on first use for a class the extension never saw) and calls manager.execute(definition, ...); the rest is container wiring. The TransactionEventDispatcher described above installs itself when the first transactional event is fired, so the interceptor carries no event code at all. TransactionScopeContext implements @TransactionScoped over the status attribute slots.

The producer classes shipped with the library (JdbcTransactionManagerProducer, PersistenceConfigurationProducer, EntityManagerFactoryProducer, JpaTransactionManagerProducer) are @ApplicationScoped so that annotated discovery sees them: @Singleton is not a bean defining annotation, so a class scoped only @Singleton would be skipped and no producer registered at all. The beans they produce stay @Singleton, because they return non-proxyable objects — a factory, the concrete manager, a mutable configuration — and the application has to be able to inject those exact types. Declaring a single ConnectionExtractor bean replaces the default extraction strategy; declaring more than one fails at startup.

• reactive / async transaction propagation
  • @Transactional on @TransactionScoped beans, timeouts, isolation levels, names
  • XA / distributed transactions, transaction suspension of a physical connection
  • nested transactions as independent transactions (only savepoint semantics)

These can be added later without reshaping the model: they are additional status kinds, additional manager hooks, or additional definition attributes.
